'''''Alcea rosea''''', the '''common hollyhock''', is an [[ornamental plant|ornamental]] [[dicot]] flowering plant in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Malvaceae]]. It was imported into Europe from southwestern China during, or possibly before, the 15th century.<ref name=harvard>{{cite web|title=Flora of China 12: 267–268. 2007|url=http://flora.huh.harvard.edu/china//PDF/PDF12/Alcea.pdf|publisher=[[Harvard University]]|access-date=2011-07-21}}</ref> [[William Turner (naturalist)|William Turner]], a [[herbalist]] of the time, gave it the name  "holyoke" from which the English name derives.

==Description==
''Alcea rosea'' is a {{Convert|8|ft|abbr=off|order=flip}} tall plant<ref name="mbg">{{cite web |title=''Alcea rosea'' (single)|publisher=[[Missouri Botanical Garden]]|url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=j240|website=missouribotanicalgarden.org|access-date=27 February 2022}}</ref> with large flowers around {{Convert|5|in|cm|order=flip}} in diameter. Its leaves are large and heart-shaped.{{cn|date=July 2026}}

== Ecology ==
The flowers attract hummingbirds in the Americas, and butterflies.<ref name="mbg" />

=== Pests and diseases ===
The leaves are vulnerable to [[Rust (fungus)|rust]], [[leaf spot]] and [[anthracnose]]. Pest problems include [[Japanese beetle]] and [[spider mites]]; though damage to the leaves can be extensive, the flowers are rarely affected.<ref name="mbg" /> In contrast, females of the hollyhock weevil (''Rhopalapion longirostre'') bore holes into the flower [[Calyx (botany)|calyx]] of the plants in which they lay their eggs. The larvae that hatch then feed upon the developing seeds, leaving each resulting pod full of desiccated husks of the seeds.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hollyhock Weevil {{!}} NC State Extension Publications|url=https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/hollyhock-weevil|website=content.ces.ncsu.edu|access-date=2026-01-30|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
[[File:Althaea rosea (Köhler).jpg|thumb|upright|Illustration, 1897]]
''Alcea rosea'' is variously described as a [[biennial plant|biennial]] (having a two-year life cycle), as an [[Annual plant|annual]], or as a short-lived [[perennial]].<ref name="cornell">{{cite web|url=https://www.gardening.cornell.edu/homegardening/scene3280.html|publisher=[[Cornell University]]|title=Hollyhock|access-date=2011-07-21}}</ref><ref name="illinois">{{cite web|url=http://urbanext.illinois.edu/hortanswers/plantdetail.cfm?PlantID=2&PlantTypeID=1|publisher=[[University of Illinois]]|title=Annual - Hollyhock - ''Althaea rosea''|access-date=2011-07-21}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://aces.nmsu.edu/county/donaana/mastergardener/documents/feb10-mg-newsltr.pdf|title=Plant of the Month - Hollyhocks|publisher=[[New Mexico State University]] Master Gardener Newsletter|access-date=2011-07-21|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111007015925/http://aces.nmsu.edu/county/donaana/mastergardener/documents/feb10-mg-newsltr.pdf|archive-date=2011-10-07}}</ref> It frequently self-sows, which may create a perception that the plants are perennial.<ref name="cornell" /> The plant may flower during its first year when sown early.<ref name="illinois" />  It will grow in a wide range of soils, and can easily reach a height of {{convert|8|ft|m|abbr=on|order=flip}}

The flowers are in a range of colours from white to dark red, including pink, yellow and orange. Different colours prefer different soils. The darker red variety seems to favour sandy soils, while the lighter colour seems to favour clay soils.{{citation needed|date=March 2013}}  The plants are easily grown from seed, and readily self-seed.  However, tender plants, whether young from seed or from old stock, may be wiped out by slugs and snails. The foliage is subject to attack from [[Puccinia malvacearum|rust fungus]], which may be treated with [[fungicide]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://plantclinic.cornell.edu/FactSheets/hollyhockrust/hollyhockrust.htm|publisher=[[Cornell University]]|title=Hollyhock rust|access-date=2009-07-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090622001430/http://plantclinic.cornell.edu/FactSheets/hollyhockrust/hollyhockrust.htm|archive-date=22 June 2009|url-status=live}}</ref> Commercial growers have reported that some closely related species (''[[Alcea ficifolia]]'' and [[Alcea rugosa|''A. rugosa'']]) are resistant to this fungus.<ref>{{cite web|title=Yard & Garden Line News|url=http://www.extension.umn.edu/yardandgarden/YGLNews/YGLN-June1505.html|publisher=[[University of Minnesota Extension]]|date=2005-06-15|access-date=2010-02-05|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100322204835/http://www.extension.umn.edu/yardandgarden/YGLNews/YGLN-June1505.html|archive-date=2010-03-22}}</ref>

==Herbalism==
In [[herbal medicine]], which may lack [[Evidence-based medicine|evidence]], hollyhock is believed to be an [[emollient]] and [[laxative]]. It is thought to control [[inflammation]], to stop [[bedwetting]] and as a mouthwash in cases of bleeding gums.<ref>Howard, Michael. ''Traditional Folk Remedies'' (Century, 1987) p.155</ref>
